query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Interlayer interfaces in multilayer HEA coatings act as effective barriers to dislocation motion and atomic diffusion, thereby reducing creep deformation, provided that interface coherence is maintained during high-temperature service.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited high-entropy multilayer protective coatings with well-defined, coherent interfaces between layers optimized to remain stable under thermal load.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of coatings: one with a multilayer architecture designed with optimized nanoscale layer thickness and controlled interface chemistry, and one monolithic HEA coating with identical overall composition; perform detailed pre- and post-creep microstructural characterization (using high-resolution TEM, EDS, etc.) to ensure interface stability.
generation.conditions: High-temperature creep conditions (600–800 °C) under controlled static loads, over durations sufficient to stress test interface integrity.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent interfaces that generate local misfit stresses and act as physical barriers to dislocation glide and atomic diffusion, verified by high-resolution microscopy before and after testing.
generation.mechanism: Dislocation and diffusion‐mediated creep are interrupted at the layer interfaces; the induced misfit stresses at these interfaces impede continuous dislocation motion and atomic rearrangements, thus reducing the overall creep strain accumulation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Multilayer coatings with stable coherent interfaces will exhibit significantly lower steady-state creep rates and higher stress exponents (indicating a shift to diffusion-controlled mechanisms) relative to monolithic coatings, as confirmed by both mechanical tests and structural observations.
generation.baseline: Monolithic high-entropy alloy coating with uniform microstructure lacking tailored interfaces.
generation.boundary: Effective when the layer thickness is maintained in the nanoscale to sub-micron range and when interfaces resist coarsening or degradation up to the operational temperatures and timescales.
generation.uncertainty: There remains uncertainty in quantitatively predicting the extent of interface degradation (e.g., coarsening or chemical changes) during prolonged high-temperature exposure, which could diminish the barrier effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct nano-indentation and uniaxial creep tests on multilayer and monolithic HEA coatings under identical high-temperature conditions; perform in-situ or sequential high-resolution TEM and EDS analyses on the interfaces before and after creep tests.
measurements: Stress exponent from log–log strain rate vs. stress plots
Interface integrity and chemical mapping via TEM/EDS after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayer coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in creep rate or if there is no evidence of dislocation interruption at interfaces when compared with the monolithic coating, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Each temperature-dependent curve in the plot can be divided into two distinct regions. Each temperature-dependent curve can be divided into two distinct stress regimes. In the low-stress regime, the extracted stress exponents fall within the diffusion-controlled range defined by Equation (4), whereas at higher stresses, the stress exponent increases markedly, indicating a transition to dislocation-dominated creep. These findings are consistent with atomic-scale observations and corroborate the proposed creep mechanism transitions. Similarly, Figure 9b shows the stress exponent n for HEA, ranging from 1.08 to 11.37. A similar stress-dependent behavior is observed for HEA, with stress exponents evolving from the diffusion-dominated regime at low stresses to dislocation-controlled deformation at higher stresses, following the same mechanistic framework as HESA. Therefore, stress-dependent creep mechanisms in HEA are essentially analogous to those observed in HESA.
